subject: music
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which musical element describes the way melodic lines or layers are combined and sound together in a piece?
questions.explain: Texture refers to how many layers of sound are heard at once and how they relate, such as melody-and-accompaniment or many independent lines.

questions.q: Which musical element refers to the relative loudness and softness of the music?
questions.explain: Dynamics cover markings such as piano (soft) and forte (loud) and how loudness changes through a piece.

questions.q: In staff notation, what does a time signature at the start of a piece indicate?
options: The number of beats in each bar and the note value that receives one beat
The key of the piece and any sharps or flats
The tempo of the piece in beats per minute
The overall dynamic level of the piece
questions.explain: For example, 3/4 shows three crotchet beats per bar, guiding the performer's metre.

questions.q: Which Italian term written in a score instructs the performer to gradually get louder?
questions.explain: Crescendo (often shown as a hairpin opening out) tells the performer to increase the volume gradually.

questions.q: A melody that uses only the five notes of a pentatonic scale is described as being:
questions.explain: A pentatonic scale has five notes per octave and is common in folk and world-music styles.

questions.q: How many pieces must a candidate submit for Component 3: Composing?
questions.explain: Candidates submit two contrasting compositions to show a range of ideas and techniques.

questions.q: Which musical element refers to the speed at which the music is played?
questions.explain: Tempo is the pace of the music, indicated by terms such as Allegro (fast) or Adagio (slow).

questions.q: What does the tempo marking 'Allegro' tell the performer?
questions.explain: Allegro is a standard Italian tempo term meaning a quick, brisk speed.

questions.q: A passage has a clear tune supported by chords underneath, all moving together in the same rhythm. This texture is best described as:
questions.explain: Homophonic texture is a melody with chordal accompaniment, where the parts largely share the same rhythm.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of notating a composition accurately as a score?
options: It allows another performer to reproduce the composer's intentions precisely
It removes the need for the composer to choose any musical elements
It guarantees the piece will use only pentatonic scales
It replaces the need to make a recording of the piece
questions.explain: A clear score communicates pitch, rhythm, dynamics and articulation so the music can be performed as the composer intended.

questions.q: In Component 3, what is meant by a 'candidate-defined brief'?
options: A set of aims and intentions the candidate sets for their own composition
A compulsory topic chosen by the exam board each year
The written score submitted alongside the recording
The mark scheme used by the examiner
questions.explain: The candidate decides the purpose, style and constraints of the piece and then composes to meet those self-set aims.

questions.q: A composition follows the plan: opening section, contrasting middle section, then a return of the opening material. What structure is this?
questions.explain: Ternary form has three sections where the third restates the first, framing a contrasting central section.

questions.q: One instrument states a melodic idea and a second instrument then repeats the same idea a little later. This device is called:
questions.explain: Imitation is when a melodic idea is echoed by another part shortly after it is first heard, creating a polyphonic texture.

questions.q: What information does a key signature at the start of each stave give the performer?
options: Which notes are consistently sharpened or flattened throughout the piece
How many beats occur in each bar
How loudly the music should be played
How fast the music should be played
questions.explain: The key signature shows the sharps or flats that apply throughout, indicating the key or tonality.

questions.q: Why is it important that the two submitted compositions are 'contrasting'?
options: To demonstrate a wider range of musical styles, elements and techniques
To ensure both pieces are in exactly the same key
To make both pieces as short as possible
To avoid having to notate either piece
questions.explain: Contrasting pieces let candidates show breadth in their handling of melody, harmony, texture, structure and timbre.

questions.q: A short rhythmic or melodic pattern is repeated persistently throughout a section of a piece. This device is called:
questions.explain: An ostinato is a repeated musical pattern that provides drive and unity beneath changing material above it.

questions.q: A candidate wants to build tension in the final section of a composition before a big release. Which combination of elements would most effectively create this rising tension?
options: A crescendo with an accelerando and increasing dissonance
A diminuendo with a ritardando and simple consonant chords
A steady quiet dynamic with a single unaccompanied melody
A sudden silence held for several bars
questions.explain: Getting louder and faster while adding clashing harmony intensifies the music towards a climax.

questions.q: A candidate wants string players to pluck the strings with their fingers rather than use the bow. Which instruction should appear in the score?
questions.explain: Pizzicato tells string players to pluck the strings; arco later cancels it and returns to bowing.

questions.q: A candidate's brief is to compose tense underscore for a film chase scene. Which approach best suits this brief?
options: Fast, driving rhythms with dissonant harmony and a growing dynamic
A slow, lyrical melody with gentle consonant chords
A simple unaccompanied pentatonic folk tune
A steady, unchanging lullaby in a major key
questions.explain: Matching musical choices to the brief, urgent rhythms and dissonance convey the tension of a chase.

questions.q: To make a repeated verse melody sound fuller and more climactic the second time it returns, a candidate could:
options: Add more instrumental layers and thicken the texture with harmony
Remove all accompaniment and leave a single quiet line
Slow the tempo right down and fade to silence
Change the piece to a completely unrelated new melody
questions.explain: Thickening the texture and adding harmony increases intensity, making the return feel like a high point.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Music (0410) syllabus; Component 3: Composing
